(sec-exudyn-cmath)=
# exudyn.cMath

The submodule `exudyn.cMath` gives Python the math functions the C++ code of Exudyn computes with: `sin`, `cos`, ..., `sqrt` and `norm`, which give the same bits on every platform. It is for the test models of Exudyn, which use it, and for everybody who wants a model to give the same results on every platform; other scripts may use `math` and `numpy` as before.

(sec-exudyn-cmath-why)=
## Why own math in Exudyn?

The transcendental functions - `sin`, `exp`, `atan2`, ... - are not correctly rounded by the libraries of the platforms, and each library rounds some results differently: the libraries of Windows and Linux differ by 1 to 3 units in the last place for between 0.1 and 55 percent of the arguments, depending on the function (#2947). A difference in the last bit is usually harmless, but models with contact, friction or impacts amplify it: a contact model gave results differing by a relative 1e-5 between Windows and Linux. Exudyn therefore compiles one portable implementation of these functions (from musl libc) into its C++ code, which gives the same bits on every platform, and `exudyn.cMath` gives the same functions to Python, for the values that enter a model: initial velocities, rotations, points of a geometry. With both, the test models of Exudyn give the same results on Windows and Linux to the last bit.

(sec-exudyn-cmath-functions)=
## Functions

Each function takes a float, which gives a float, or a list or numpy array, which gives a numpy array of the same shape; the two arguments of `atan2` and `pow` are broadcast like numpy does. A call with one float takes about 0.2 microseconds, against 0.03 of `math.sin`; on arrays the functions are as fast as numpy. `sqrt` is correctly rounded on every platform, also in `math` and `numpy`; it is here so that one import serves. Python's `x**0.5` and `x**y` call the library's `pow` and differ per platform: use `sqrt`, or `pow` of this module. A complex array is not supported: it loses its imaginary part, with the ComplexWarning of numpy.

Usage: `from exudyn.cMath import sin, cos, pi`, or `import exudyn.cMath as cm` and `cm.sin(x)`. The functions are:
- **`sin(x)`**: sine of x (in radians); calls EM::Sin of the C++ code
- **`cos(x)`**: cosine of x (in radians); calls EM::Cos of the C++ code
- **`tan(x)`**: tangent of x (in radians); calls EM::Tan of the C++ code
- **`asin(x)`**: arc sine of x in [-1,1], in [-pi/2, pi/2]; calls EM::Asin of the C++ code
- **`acos(x)`**: arc cosine of x in [-1,1], in [0, pi]; calls EM::Acos of the C++ code
- **`atan(x)`**: arc tangent of x, in [-pi/2, pi/2]; calls EM::Atan of the C++ code
- **`exp(x)`**: exponential function of x; calls EM::Exp of the C++ code
- **`log(x)`**: natural logarithm of x; calls EM::Log of the C++ code
- **`sinh(x)`**: hyperbolic sine of x; calls EM::Sinh of the C++ code
- **`cosh(x)`**: hyperbolic cosine of x; calls EM::Cosh of the C++ code
- **`tanh(x)`**: hyperbolic tangent of x; calls EM::Tanh of the C++ code
- **`cbrt(x)`**: cube root of x, also for a negative x; calls EM::Cbrt of the C++ code
- **`sqrt(x)`**: square root of x; correctly rounded on every platform; calls std::sqrt of the C++ code
- **`atan2(y, x)`**: arc tangent of y/x in [-pi, pi], with the quadrant of the point (x, y); y is the FIRST argument, as in math.atan2; calls EM::Atan2 of the C++ code
- **`pow(x, y)`**: x to the power y; calls EM::Pow of the C++ code
- **`pi`**: the float closest to pi, the same as math.pi; defined in python/exudyn/cMath.py
- **`norm(x)`**: the Euclidean norm of a vector, or the Frobenius norm of a matrix: the square root of the sum of the squares, added by math.fsum without rounding before the end; numpy.linalg.norm sums in an order that depends on the BLAS library and the CPU (#2963); defined in python/exudyn/cMath.py
